pages.text: It was the first week of school, and the autumn mornings were still warm. Noah walked to school with his big cousin. She was ten, and she knew every street in the city. She also had a game. At every crossing, Noah was the leader.
pages.speech: It was the first week of school, and the autumn mornings were still warm. Noah walked to school with his big cousin. She was ten, and she knew every street in the city. She also had a game. At every crossing, Noah was the leader.

pages.text: At the first crossing, Noah stopped at the kerb. He looked one way, then the other way, then the first way again. The little man in the light was red, so he waited. When the green man lit up, Noah walked across. He did not run. “Stop, look, look, look, walk,” he said proudly.
pages.speech: At the first crossing, Noah stopped at the kerb. He looked one way, then the other way, then the first way again. The little man in the light was red, so he waited. When the green man lit up, Noah walked across. He did not run. “Stop, look, look, look, walk,” he said proudly.

pages.text: At the second crossing, a bus rumbled past and a car hooted. Noah stopped. Look, look, look. Wait for green. Walk. “Easy,” he said, and he felt very tall. His cousin smiled and said nothing. She just walked one step behind him.
pages.speech: At the second crossing, a bus rumbled past and a car hooted. Noah stopped. Look, look, look. Wait for green. Walk. “Easy,” he said, and he felt very tall. His cousin smiled and said nothing. She just walked one step behind him.

pages.text: Noah listened to the city as they walked. He heard the buses before he saw them. He heard the motorbikes buzzing and the cars humming round the corner. “I can hear everything coming,” he told his cousin. “I don’t even need to look.”

pages.text: The last crossing was a small one, by the bakery. There was no traffic light there, only white stripes on the road. The bakery smelled of warm bread. Noah stopped at the kerb, just like before, and listened. No engines. No buses. Nothing.
pages.speech: The last crossing was a small one, by the bakery. There was no traffic light there, only white stripes on the road. The bakery smelled of warm bread. Noah stopped at the kerb, just like before, and listened. No engines. No buses. Nothing.

pages.text: “Nothing coming!” said Noah. He lifted his foot to step off the kerb. His cousin put a hand on his shoulder. “Look too,” she said quietly. Noah sighed, because he was sure. But he looked.
pages.speech: “Nothing coming!” said Noah. He lifted his foot to step off the kerb. His cousin put a hand on his shoulder. “Look too,” she said quietly. Noah sighed, because he was sure. But he looked.

pages.text: Something was coming. A bicycle with a small electric motor glided past, quick and silent, right where his foot would have been. There was no engine sound at all, only a soft hiss of tyres. Noah’s heart jumped into his throat.
pages.speech: Something was coming. A bicycle with a small electric motor glided past, quick and silent, right where his foot would have been. There was no engine sound at all, only a soft hiss of tyres. Noah’s heart jumped into his throat.

pages.text: “Sorry!” called the rider over her shoulder, and she was gone round the corner. Noah stood very still on the kerb. His cousin kept her hand on his shoulder. For a moment, neither of them said anything.
pages.speech: “Sorry!” called the rider over her shoulder, and she was gone round the corner. Noah stood very still on the kerb. His cousin kept her hand on his shoulder. For a moment, neither of them said anything.

pages.text: “I didn’t hear it,” said Noah in a small voice. “Not at all.” “Me neither,” said his cousin. “Some things are very quiet.” Noah looked at the road. It looked empty. Quiet, he thought, is not the same as empty.

pages.text: Noah took a deep breath. Stop. He looked one way. He looked the other way. He looked the first way again, very carefully. Nothing was coming, really nothing this time. Walk. They crossed together, past the warm smell of bread.
pages.speech: Noah took a deep breath. Stop. He looked one way. He looked the other way. He looked the first way again, very carefully. Nothing was coming, really nothing this time. Walk. They crossed together, past the warm smell of bread.

pages.text: At the school gate, Noah’s cousin grinned at him. “You were a good leader,” she said. “Tomorrow you can lead the whole way, from our door to this gate.” Noah stood up very straight. “And I’ll look every time,” he said. “Even when it’s quiet.”

pages.text: The next morning, Noah led the whole way. At every crossing he stopped, looked, looked, looked and waited. He looked even when the street was quiet. Especially when the street was quiet. His cousin walked one step behind him, humming.

pages.text: At the bakery crossing, Noah stopped and looked. The street was quiet, but this time he saw it in good time: the electric bicycle, coming slowly. The rider saw them too. She stopped before the white stripes and smiled. “After you,” she said.

pages.text: Noah looked the other way too, just to be sure. Then he crossed, walking, not running. At the school gate, his cousin bowed like a knight. “Thank you, Leader,” she said. Noah laughed. Stop, look, look, look, walk. It was his rule now.

activity.title: Map My Way
activity.goal: Draw and read a simple map.

steps.caption: Walk a short way together. Hold hands at every crossing.
At home, draw the map: your door, the streets, the place.
Light or no light? Mark each crossing.
Walk it again with the map. You show the way.

activity.safety: The adult holds the child’s hand at every crossing, both walks. The child never crosses alone. Look at the map only while standing still on the pavement, never while crossing. Choose a short, quiet route and walk it in daylight. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Noah learns to stop at the kerb and look both ways every time, even when he hears nothing, because some vehicles, such as electric bicycles and scooters, are almost silent. This activity takes the same streets home and turns them into a map. Choose a short route you already walk together, such as to the shop, the park or school. On the first walk, stop together at every crossing and let the child do Noah’s rule out loud: stop at the kerb, look one way, the other way, the first way again, wait for the green light where there is one, and walk. Hold the child’s hand at every crossing. Children of this age still need an adult beside them when they cross. At home, the child draws the map: your front door at one end, the place at the other, the streets as lines in between. Then the child draws stripes wherever you crossed. Ask: “Which crossings had a traffic light? Which did not?” Let them mark the difference in their own way, perhaps a small light or a pair of eyes. Before the second walk, ask the child to predict which crossing needs the most care, and why. Then walk the route again with the map in hand: the child shows the way, and you still hold their hand at every kerb. Praise careful looking (“you looked even when it was quiet”), not speed. Thirty minutes is about right, or split it over two days. To make it easier, draw only the walk from your door to the first corner. To make it harder, add landmarks such as a tree or a shop, or draw the way back too.
activity.inClass: The class walks once round the school block with the teacher and enough adults to hold hands at every crossing. Back in class, groups of four draw the walk together on one big sheet and mark every crossing, with or without a light. Each group then shows its map and explains which crossing needs the most care. Display the maps on the wall.
